title: Character Traits and Motivation
keyIdea: A trait is what a character is like most of the time, such as brave, honest or selfish; a feeling is how they feel at one moment, such as scared or cross, and it can change by the next page. Writers usually show traits instead of naming them, so the proof is what a character does and says, never their looks. A motivation is the reason behind an action, what the character wants or fears, and a good reader backs it with a clue from the story instead of judging the whole person from one action. Traits come in amounts, so weigh all the evidence. The narrator may tell you what to think of a character, but you can hold your own view if you can point to evidence for it.
familyTip: At bedtime, pick one character from the story you are reading. Ask: what is one word for what they are like, and what did they do that proves it? Then ask why they did one thing in the story, and hunt together for the clue earlier on that explains it.

visual.caption: Trait or feeling? Drag each word, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort traits from feelings, match evidence to traits, find motives from clues, place a trait on a scale, split narrator from opinion.

kid: A trait is what a character is like most of the time. Brave, kind and honest are traits. A feeling is how they feel right now, like scared or cross. A feeling can change by the next page.
Writers do not often say a character is kind. They show it. Look at what the character does and says. That is your proof. How they look does not prove what they are like inside.
A motive is why a character does something. It is what they want or what they fear. Find a clue in the story that explains it. Do not decide a character is bad from one thing they do.
The narrator may tell you what to think. You can see it a different way. Just point to what the character does to show why.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. The US Common Core asks Grade 3 readers to describe characters by their traits, motives and feelings (RL.3.3). They also explain how a character's actions drive the events. RL.3.6 asks them to tell their own point of view from the narrator's. In England, Year 3 and 4 readers infer feelings, thoughts and motives from actions, and back each inference with evidence.

Three ideas carry the topic. A trait lasts and a feeling passes, so cross after a broken bike is not a cross person. Traits are inferred from actions and speech, not from looks or a label. A motive links an action to a want or a fear hinted at earlier in the text. Good answers name that clue.

Common mistakes: treating a feeling as a trait; using looks as evidence, as if curly hair shows character; judging the whole person from one action, such as calling Ben mean when the story says his dog is lost; guessing a motive with no clue in the text; and taking the narrator's label on trust without checking what the character does.

In the lab your child sorts ten words into trait or feeling and matches eight clues about Tomas to a trait. They pick the motive a clue supports for four characters and drag a marker along four trait scales. Then they sort lines about Mrs Grey into narrator, evidence and opinion, and choose the strongest proof for four claims.

practice.prompt: Which word is a trait, not a feeling?
practice.hint: A trait is what someone is like most of the time.
practice.explain: patient describes someone most of the time, so it is a trait. nervous and sleepy are feelings that come and go.

practice.prompt: Asha finds {n} clues about a character. {k} of them are only about how the character looks. How many clues can prove a trait?
practice.hint: Looks do not prove a trait. Take those away.
practice.explain: {n} − {k} = {=n-k} clues are actions or words, so they can prove a trait.

practice.prompt: Best proof that Finn is generous:
choices: He shared his crayons with the whole table.
His mum said he was a good boy.
practice.hint: Which one is something Finn does?
practice.explain: Sharing is an action that shows generous. A smile is how he looks, and his mum's words are a label, not proof.

practice.prompt: For each of {c} characters you write one trait and {e} pieces of evidence. How many pieces of evidence do you write?
practice.explain: {c} × {e} = {=c*e} pieces of evidence, each one an action or something the character says.

practice.prompt: Earlier the story says Leo wants to be picked as class helper. Why does he stay late to tidy?
choices: He hopes to be chosen as helper.
practice.hint: Use the clue from earlier in the story.
practice.explain: The clue says Leo wants to be helper, so tidying is his way to be chosen. The other reasons have no clue in the story.

pool.prompt: Zara is cross because her bike broke. What is cross here?
pool.hint: Will Zara still be cross next week?
pool.explain: cross is how Zara feels at that moment, so it is a feeling. It does not mean she is a cross person.

pool.prompt: Ben snaps at his best friend. That morning his dog went missing. Which is the fairest reading?
choices: Ben is worried, so he is snappy today.
pool.hint: Is there a clue that explains the action?
pool.explain: The lost dog is the clue: Ben is worried. Calling him mean judges his whole character from one action.

pool.prompt: Which clue proves Kim is determined?
choices: She tried the puzzle ten times until it fitted.
pool.hint: Determined means keeping going. Find the action.
pool.explain: Trying ten times shows determined. A favourite colour shows nothing, and nice is a label about a different trait.

pool.prompt: The narrator says Mrs Grey is grumpy, but she leaves water out for every stray cat. Which is your own opinion?
choices: I think she is lonely, not grumpy.
She leaves water out for cats.
pool.hint: An opinion often starts with I think.
pool.explain: I think she is lonely is your view. The cats line is evidence from the story, and the grumpy line is the narrator's view.

pool.prompt: A trait scale runs from shy to outgoing. {a} clues show shy and {b} clues show outgoing. How many clues do you weigh in all?
pool.hint: Weigh every clue, not just one side.
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} clues. You look at all of them before you place the marker.

pool.prompt: Amira gives her prize to her little brother, who cried all week about losing. What is her motive?
choices: She wants to cheer him up.
pool.hint: What clue does the story give about her brother?
pool.explain: Her brother was upset, so she wants to cheer him up. The other reasons are guesses with no clue.

pool.prompt: Sam keeps the ball at first, then shares it with everyone. Where does he sit between mean and kind?
pool.hint: Do the two clues point the same way?
pool.explain: One clue shows mean and one shows kind, so he sits in the middle. Weigh all the evidence, not one line.

pool.prompt: In a story, {t} sentences name a character's trait outright and {s} show it through actions. How many sentences give evidence you can quote?
pool.hint: Both kinds are in the story text, so both can be quoted.
pool.explain: {t} + {s} = {=t+s} sentences you can quote, but the {s} that show actions are the stronger proof.

pool.prompt: Which question helps you find a character's motive?
choices: What does the character want or fear?
pool.hint: A motive is the reason behind an action.
pool.explain: A motive is what the character wants or fears. Clothes and the author's age do not explain why the character acts.

pool.prompt: Which word describes a feeling, not a trait?
pool.hint: Which one could be gone by teatime?
pool.explain: embarrassed is a feeling at one moment. honest and selfish describe someone most of the time.
